Not financial advice

This tool is for informational and educational purposes only. It does not provide financial, tax, legal, or investment advice, and nothing it produces should be relied on to make financial decisions — it's arithmetic on whatever assumptions you type in. Tax here is a graduated federal and provincial approximation, not the Income Tax Act: most credits and several province-specific rules are absent. Every default on this form is a placeholder, not a typical number. Consult a qualified, licensed professional before acting on anything you see here.

Privacy, and no AI in the maths

The numbers you type never leave your browser — there is no server behind this page, no account and no analytics, and nothing you enter is uploaded, stored or transmitted anywhere. Saved plans live in this browser alone; exporting to a file is the reliable way to keep them, because clearing browser data wipes the rest. Download this file, disconnect from the internet, open it, and it still works.

Nothing here asks a language model what your money does. Every figure comes from arithmetic written out in the source of this file — brackets, rates and rules you can read, in order, and check against the CRA's own tables. The file was written with AI assistance, as most software now is; the calculation itself contains none, makes no network request of any kind, and gives the same answer every time from the same inputs.

What this does not model

Tax here is a graduated federal and provincial approximation, not the Income Tax Act: most credits and several province-specific rules are absent. Ontario's two-tier surtax and its health premium ARE charged, and so is the federal basic-amount phase-out above $181,440; the low-income reductions in New Brunswick, PEI and Nova Scotia are not. Nor are CPP and EI premiums on earnings, so the years you are still working come out somewhat better than a pay stub. Within that, the gaps worth knowing are the ones no tooltip mentions. The age amount, the pension income amount and the disability amount are all claimed for you where you qualify — the disability amount on the basis that an RDSP beneficiary is eligible for it, so a household with no RDSP does not get it even if someone would in real life. Eligible pension income here means a workplace pension at any age and a required RRIF withdrawal from 65; a RRIF you converted early, between 65 and 71, is not counted, so the pension amount can be understated in those years. A couple can split eligible pension income between them (form T1032), which is worth real money when one of you has most of the pension; it is on by default, the amount moved is shown in the table, and the Pension section has the switch. The model picks the transfer that minimises your combined tax and OAS recovery each year, which is what a preparer's software does — but it decides one year at a time, so it will not sacrifice this year to set up a better next one. CPP pays a survivor's own retirement pension and their survivor benefit as ONE combined amount that cannot exceed the maximum retirement pension, and that cap is applied here from age 65 — so if both of you have high CPP the survivor can receive less than the top-up percentage you entered, or none of it. Below 65 a different survivor formula applies that is not modelled here. The Guaranteed Income Supplement IS paid where you qualify, on last year's income excluding OAS and GIS, which is the real rule — so a large withdrawal shows up as a smaller supplement the year after, not the same year. Watch what that costs: in the middle of the range a dollar taken from an RRSP gives back about 75 cents of next year's supplement on top of the tax on it, and the drawdown order here does not rearrange itself to avoid that. The Allowance and the Allowance for the Survivor, paid between 60 and 64 and worth up to $1,448.06 and $1,726.18 a month, are NOT included — this page never asks the questions that decide who is eligible, so if either might apply to you the real answer is better than the one below. Every dividend is treated as an eligible Canadian one, so foreign dividends belong in the interest box instead. Non-registered holdings carry a single pooled cost base per person rather than one per security. Selling below that cost base realizes a capital loss, which is carried forward against later gains — never back against gains already taxed, and never against other income while you are alive. There is no superficial-loss rule, and gains accrue untaxed until sold — which fits a buy-and-hold ETF holder and flatters a fund that distributes gains yearly. On the RDSP, the taxable share of a plan you already hold rests on the one percentage you enter rather than a real contribution history; provincial disability benefits and their income tests are not modelled at all; and there is no Canada Disability Savings Bond calculation, so low-income years that would attract it earn nothing here.

Source, and where to report a problem

The whole calculator is one file, and this is it — nothing is fetched, so what you are reading is what ran. Source, releases and issues: github.com/christhefarmer/runway. A wrong number is worth reporting even if you are not certain: say which fields you entered and what you expected, and it can be checked against the tax tables. Bracket and benefit figures are re-verified periodically, and the date they were last checked is shown above the Forecast table.

CRA tables Federal and provincial brackets, CPP, OAS and RRIF minimums for the tax year shown above the Forecast table. Verified on the date printed there.
